seal.title: Encrypt this page?
seal.body: Title, text, look, map, choice, module content and menu will be encrypted in the browser. The server will see only the address, that the page exists and how many modules it has. The page key goes to people with access to its areas and to the role that runs it.
seal.form: People from a form (without an account) will see the page only once the form gives them a role with one of these areas and someone from the office passes them the key.
seal.single: A module from this page can't stand on any other page.
seal.lost: If all keys are lost, the page can't be read — a database backup won't restore it.
seal.files: Images and files of this page are not encrypted (yet).
seal.check: Encrypted — only people with the key of its areas read the page's content; the server doesn't know it (images and files are not encrypted yet)
seal.needKey: Encryption needs the account key — sign in again.
seal.unwrapped: Without the page key: {areas}. People only from these areas won't open it until someone with their key renews the page key.
seal.openArea: The area {areas} is open — anyone can fetch its key, so encryption hides nothing from anyone.

unseal.title: Turn off encryption for this page?
unseal.body: The page stays access-only, but its content will be stored openly again — as before encryption.

json.title: Import and export (JSON)
json.lead: Aliases and own domains — to copy or to have prepared by an AI. The import creates new aliases and connects, swaps or (with "host": null) disconnects domains; it neither changes nor removes existing aliases. The plan also says what is left to do outside the platform.

key.pages: export info only: addresses of pages you run — only they can be an alias target ("target") and a domain's page ("path"); "" is recreatio.pl itself
key.roles: export info only: your roles that can be responsible for an alias (below)
key.roleId: role id — used by an alias's "role"
key.roleName: role name, as you see it in the workshop
key.aliasPath: alias address without "recreatio.pl/", e.g. "parafia/news": lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, parts separated by a slash; it must lie UNDER an address you run (a top-level address like "cogita" is issued by the server with a code); by it the import recognises an alias that already exists
key.aliasTarget: address of the page the alias leads to — one of "pages" (not another alias: there are no chains)
key.aliasRole: who is responsible for the alias: an "id" from "roles"; left out — the role that runs the target page
key.domainPath: the page the domain shows — one of "pages" (a page has at most one domain); by it the import recognises a domain that already exists
key.domainHost: just the domain name, e.g. "cogita.pl": lowercase letters, with a dot, without "https://" and without a path (up to 200 characters); different from the current one — replaces it; null — disconnects the domain from this page (the only way of removing in this format)

outside.dns: DNS at the domain registrar: A for the bare domain → {a}; AAAA → {aaaa}; CNAME for “www” → {cname}.
outside.host: A separate place for the site's files under this name: GitHub Pages accepts one own domain per repository, and that one is already recreatio.pl — a separate repository with a CNAME file or other static file hosting is needed.
outside.origin: The service's consent: the domain name in “Api:Origins” of the api.recreatio.pl service — set by the server administrator; without it the page under the domain won't read data.

json.usageTitle: How the app uses this data
json.usage:
- An alias and a domain are just a second entrance: the service leads them to the target page and takes everything from there — title, introduction, modules, look. A change to the page is visible at once under every entrance.
- Under an own domain subpages have shorter addresses: on cogita.pl the page cogita/kursy is #/kursy.
- Access follows the target page: an access-only page (sealed too) stays so under an alias and under a domain, and one blocked after a report shows under no entrance.
- Nobody gets new rights: the page is still edited by those who run its address. An alias's "role" only says who manages it — not who sees the page.
- An alias is not a separate page: where a page is chosen (e.g. for access links) it doesn't appear — the target page is chosen. The dependency map shows the domain next to its page.
json.formatTitle: Addresses and domains as JSON ("{format}", version {version})
json.intro:
Aliases and own domains of the pages this account runs (Workshop → Settings → “Addresses and domains” → “Import and export (JSON)”, #/workspace/addresses). An alias is a second entrance to a page inside recreatio.pl (recreatio.pl/parafia/news shows parafia/aktualnosci); an own domain shows a page under another name (cogita.pl shows recreatio.pl/cogita). The content stays where it lies — the entrance only points to it.
What the import does:
- It first shows the plan of changes with warnings; it saves only after “Import”.
- An alias that doesn't exist yet is created. An alias that exists is recognised by "path": the same target — no change; a different target — a warning (an alias's target can't be changed nor an alias removed — in the app either).
- It connects a domain to the page "path", swaps it for another or — only with "host": null — disconnects it. Moving a domain to another page: at the old page "host": null (or another domain), at the new one this domain — the import first disconnects, then connects.
- Pages not in "domains" and aliases not in "aliases" stay unchanged. It removes nothing else.
- It doesn't take addresses: a top-level address (e.g. recreatio.pl/cogita) is issued by the server with a code — “Pages” → “Take an address”.
What remains outside the app — for each new domain (the plan reminds of it on import):
{outside}
Signing in under an own domain also needs api.{host} (a CNAME to the same service, with a certificate) — also work on the server; public pages work without it.
Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

how.title: How it works
how.root: An address taken with a code is a root. parish is taken once, with a code from the server. Everything below it — parish/grzegorzki — is opened by whoever runs it, in the workshop and without a code. Such routes can't be taken separately, and that's on purpose: otherwise one address would have two people responsible, and which page a visitor sees would depend on the order of rows in the database.
how.local: Sub-routes are local. If cogita.pl shows recreatio.pl/cogita, the page cogita/kursy is available under that domain as cogita.pl/#/kursy — without repeating the root name. That's why links on a page are written locally: the same link works both under recreatio.pl and under the own domain. If it contained the full path, one of the two versions would always be broken.
how.alias: An alias is a second entrance, not a second page. Nothing is saved under an alias — title, introduction and modules change where the content lies. The service refuses to save to an alias whether or not someone took it: two versions of the same thing would mean that one of them is out of date.

out.title: What has to be done outside the platform
out.lead: Connecting a domain here saves only one thing: that this name means this page. For a browser to get here at all, three more things are needed that aren't in the database.
out.hostTitle: 2. The same site under the new name
out.host: GitHub Pages accepts one own domain per repository, and that one is already recreatio.pl. A second domain therefore needs its own place: a separate repository with its own CNAME file or any static file hosting. An entry in the registry alone won't do it.
out.originTitle: 3. The service's consent to the new name
out.origin: A browser won't let a page from cogita.pl read answers from api.recreatio.pl until the service lists that name (Api:Origins). That takes someone with access to the server — it isn't set in the workshop, and that's how it should be: the list of allowed names is part of the security, not of the content.
out.loginTitle: Signing in under an own domain
out.login: Public pages work without signing in — the visitor needs nothing, point 3 is enough. But signing in under an own domain is harder: the session cookie is issued by api.recreatio.pl, so on cogita.pl it is a third-party cookie, and Safari and Firefox block or partition those. The session simply won't come back.
out.ways: There are two ways. The simpler: under the own domain only show the page, and manage it on recreatio.pl — there the cookie is first-party. The full one: point api.your-domain (a CNAME record) to the same service and build the software there with VITE_APP_API=https://api.your-domain. Then service and page are under one name, the cookie is first-party and signing in works. It needs a certificate for that subdomain — also work on the server.
